title: Designing a Privacy‑First VS Code Extension: Lessons from CodeLoom Explorer
excerpt: Creating a tool that visualizes code dependencies without leaving the editor required balancing AST parsing, React Flow, and a strict no‑network policy.

content.text: When I started building CodeLoom Explorer, my goal was simple: give developers a quick way to see how files in a project relate to each other, without having to leave the editor or trust a third‑party service.
I wanted the extension to work entirely offline. That meant no sending file contents to a remote server, no API keys, and no telemetry. It also meant I had to handle parsing on the client side.
I used TypeScript and the compiler API to build an AST for each file, then walked the tree to extract import/export relationships.
For the visual part, I chose React Flow. It gave me out‑of‑the‑box pan, zoom, and node dragging, which let me focus on the data model rather than canvas drawing.
Each file became a node, and each import became a directed edge. To keep the graph readable, I added clustering for directories and a search box that highlights related nodes.
Parsing every file on every save would be too slow for large repos. I introduced a watcher that only re‑parses changed files and caches the AST in IndexedDB.
When the graph grows beyond a few thousand nodes, I switch to a simplified view that groups files by folder, preserving the overall structure without overwhelming the UI.
The best developer tools are invisible until you need them, then they feel like they were always there.
content.author: Unknown

content.text: The biggest surprise was how often developers ask for a 'quick overview' but then need to drill down into specific modules. The extension's filtering and focus modes turned out to be more valuable than the initial graph view.

I also learned that building for VS Code means respecting its extension model: keep the extension lightweight, handle activation events carefully, and always provide a way to disable the feature if it becomes distracting.
Looking ahead, I'm exploring adding a 'dependency impact' view that predicts which files are most likely to break when a change is made, using simple static analysis.
